title: Capturing Thought Dynamics: Modeling the Structure of Spontaneous Associations
short_title: Capturing thought dynamics: free associations and repetitive thinking

affiliations.b: The Gonda Multidisciplinary Brain Research Center, Bar-Ilan University
affiliations.c: Department of Information Systems, University of Haifa

abstract: Human thought unfolds in patterns that vary across individuals; some move fluidly across ideas, whereas others return to narrower or more repetitive paths. Here, we asked whether structural aspects of associative thinking—its breadth, trajectory, and temporal pace—can account for individual differences in repetitive thought styles such as rumination. Participants completed brief free-association tasks, and their responses were quantified using a model trained on large-scale free association data to derive individual structural profiles of associative flow. Across two independent samples, these profiles predicted self-reported measures of rumination and repetitive thinking, with nonlinear models accounting for meaningful inter-individual variation and showing generalization across tasks and datasets. These findings suggest that individual differences in repetitive thought are reflected not only in what people think about but also in how associations are organized and unfold over time. Structural modeling therefore provides a viable approach to characterizing spontaneous cognition through patterns of associative organization.
summary: Can the way thoughts move from one idea to the next, rather than what they are about, tell us something about a tendency to ruminate? We built the Associator, a model trained on about 126,000 Hebrew word-association pairs, to score how strong each associative link is, and used it to describe how people’s free associations unfold. The associative measures had no linear relation to rumination and repetitive-thinking questionnaires, but nonlinear models predicted the questionnaire scores, and models trained on a first sample still did so in an independent sample. How associations are organized may be a useful window on repetitive thought, alongside what people think about.
key_findings: The Associator estimated the associative strength of unseen word pairs with a mean prediction error of 2.98%, about 0.3 points on its 0–10 scale.
The associative measures (breadth, trajectory and response time) showed no linear relation to the rumination and repetitive-thinking questionnaires.

In Experiment I (97 undergraduates), nonlinear Converter models gave predicted scores practically equivalent to the observed ones for all six task–questionnaire pairs; control models trained on random targets did not.
Applied unchanged to an independent sample of 213 adults, the models met the equivalence criterion in three of four pairs and their predictions explained 46–60% of the variance.
The data are Hebrew, the samples mostly female and non-clinical, and the measures self-reported; other languages and clinical populations are still to be tested.
